knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we express

$$
f(x)=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{4}.
$$

Now, we see that $f(x)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
f={u}^{4},\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=4{u}^{3}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =4{u}^{3}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-4{u}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-4{cos}^{3}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$
